today: ARPAWOCKY is a historical record of early ARPANET culture and the vocabulary that dominated the research community in 1973. It shows that the ARPANET community had humor and self-awareness about the technical complexity they were building. Many of the terms referenced (NCP, RFNM, DDT) are now obsolete, making the poem also a time capsule of forgotten protocols. It has not been obsoleted, and reading it now provides insight into how ARPANET researchers thought about their network.

sections.title: ARPAWOCKY: A Network Parody
sections.content:
RFC 527, titled ARPAWOCKY, is a humorous poem by R. Merryman that parodies Lewis Carroll's famous Jabberwocky from Through the Looking-Glass. The parody keeps the original poem's nonsense-verse structure and rhythm but replaces the fantasy setting and creatures with ARPANET terminology, acronyms, and concepts.

The poem has no technical content and serves as a cultural artifact: a playful record of the jargon and concerns that occupied the minds of early ARPANET researchers.
sections.eli5: Someone took a famous nonsense poem and rewrote it using all the confusing computer terms people used on the early network. It's funny because the jargon is so thick and strange.

sections.title: ARPANET Terms in Verse
sections.content:
The poem references many real ARPANET concepts: USER-SERVER describes the client-server relationship; FTP (File Transfer Protocol) and RJE (Remote Job Entry) are file and job transmission protocols; NCP (Network Control Protocol) is the predecessor to TCP; IMPs are the Interface Message Processors that route packets; RFNM is a Request For Next Message, an acknowledgment; Echo-plex is a teletype feature for local echo.

The poem's hero takes his coding pad, struggles with the HOST-to-IMP connection, watches the ARPANET send packets with ACK and NACK messages, and celebrates joining the network. The tone is playful and self-aware about the technical complexity.
sections.eli5: The poem uses real ARPANET words like FTP and IMP but puts them in a poem where they sound like they're from a fantasy adventure. It's a joke that pokes fun at how much jargon the network people used.

sections.title: A Window on Early ARPANET Culture
sections.content: ARPAWOCKY is valuable not for technical content but as a cultural artifact. It captures the vocabulary and concerns of the ARPANET research community: protocols (USER-SERVER, FTP, RJE, NCP), network hardware (IMPs, TIPs), the bits and bytes that make up messages, and the acknowledgments (ACK, NACK) that govern reliable communication. The poet's affectionate tone toward the ARPANET, with its monsters and challenges, reflects how researchers thought about their network as a living system.
sections.eli5: This poem is like a time machine. It shows what ARPANET people cared about and how they talked about their work.
